claims.text: The baseline system is an elemental Cr coating on a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate.
An ultrathin Al-doped modification layer can be incorporated within or on top of the elemental Cr coating.
Adding the Al-doped layer will promote in situ formation of dense Al2O3.
High-temperature steam exposure will form a stable Al2O3 scale at the Cr/substrate interface.
The resulting Al2O3 barrier will be continuous, adherent, and dense.
Incorporated Al will oxidize preferentially to form Al2O3.
Al2O3 is chemically stable at the specified high temperatures.
A dense Al2O3 phase will act as a diffusion barrier that suppresses Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve the integrity of the Cr coating during accident conditions.
The alumina barrier will be thin enough not to disrupt the protective behavior of the Cr layer during normal operation.
The Al-modified Cr coating will retain the Cr-based protective function under normal subcritical-water operation.
Normal PWR subcritical-water operation is bounded here at temperatures below 400°C.
Accident-relevant testing is bounded at approximately 800–1000°C in steam for exposures on the order of hours, including up to 5 hours.
Relative to pure Cr coating, the Al-modified coating will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
Relative to pure Cr coating, the Al-modified coating will delay the onset of coating degradation during high-temperature steam exposure.
The Al-modified coating will maintain adequate protection during subcritical-water operation.

contradictions.description: The Al-doped layer is variously located within the Cr coating, on top of it, and at the Cr/substrate interface. These locations are not equivalent, and no transport or processing step is given to explain how a surface or intracoating Al layer produces an interfacial alumina barrier.
